scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a two-view response that weighs interest against job availability and lets both guide the choice; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Picking a field of study is one of the biggest decisions a young person faces.
Some believe students should consider only their own talents and interests, while others believe they should base the choice on the availability of jobs.
I believe both matter, and that the wisest choice weighs personal interest together with job prospects.

sections.role: Body 1 — Why talents and interests matter

sentences.text: First, a student's own talents and interests deserve serious weight.
People usually do their best work in a field they genuinely care about.
For example, a student passionate about science will study harder and achieve more than a bored one.
This shows that interest and talent often lead to both success and satisfaction.
Choosing a field with no personal interest can lead to a dull and joyless career.
Following our talents also lets us contribute what we are truly best at.
To this extent, talents and interests should guide the choice.
Second, however, the availability of jobs cannot simply be ignored.
A student must be able to earn a living once her studies are finished.
Consider a graduate with a beloved degree but no job prospects, struggling for years under debt.
Such hardship shows that ignoring the job market can lead to real suffering.
Knowing where jobs exist helps students plan a secure and stable future.
Job markets also change, so combining passion with practical skills is the safest path.
Both views, then, point to needs that a wise choice must balance.
In conclusion, students should certainly follow their talents and interests.
But they should also consider job prospects, since they must earn a living.
The wisest students choose a field where their interests and their prospects can meet.
